name: Local Outlier Factor (LOF)
analogy: Think of it as judging a house by its own street. A lone house in a crowded city block looks out of place, while the same spacing in the countryside is normal. The model compares how crowded a bar's surroundings are with how crowded its neighbours' surroundings are, so what counts as strange depends on the neighbourhood.

steps.title: Describe every bar as a point
steps.description: Each bar becomes a point in a space whose axes are the chosen features, after scaling them to comparable sizes. Bars that behave alike sit close together and unusual bars sit apart.
steps.inExample: Each 5-minute bar becomes a point described by three scaled features: range against average true range, volume ratio and the move from open to close.

steps.title: Find each bar's nearest neighbours
steps.description: For every bar the model finds a fixed number of nearest other bars. That number is the main setting: small values look at very local structure, larger ones look at wider neighbourhoods.
steps.inExample: With the neighbour count set to 20, each bar is linked to its 20 closest bars.

steps.title: Measure how crowded each bar's surroundings are
steps.description: It measures how far a bar has to reach to touch its neighbours. A bar whose neighbours are close by lives in a dense area, and one that must reach far lives in a sparse area. This gives each bar a local crowdedness.
steps.inExample: The bar in question reaches about 2 scaled units to touch its 20 neighbours, whereas its neighbours typically reach about 1 scaled unit.

steps.title: Compare with the neighbours' crowdedness
steps.description: The bar's crowdedness is compared with the crowdedness of each of its neighbours. If the bar is about as crowded as the bars around it, it fits in; if it is much more spread out than they are, it is a local outlier.
steps.inExample: The bar is about twice as spread out as its neighbours, so its comparison ratio is about 2.

steps.title: Read the ratio as the outlier factor
steps.description: A ratio near 1 means normal, a ratio well above 1 means the bar is more isolated than its surroundings, and a value under 1 means it sits in an unusually tight spot. There is no universal cutoff, so one is picked from the scores.
steps.inExample: A ratio of about 2 is far above 1; typical bars score close to 1.

steps.title: Choose the flagging cutoff
steps.description: Bars above the chosen cutoff are marked as outliers. A cutoff can be a fixed ratio or the top few percent of scores in the training data.
steps.inExample: The cutoff is set to the top 1 percent of scores, which falls at about 1 and a half, so this bar is flagged.

steps.title: Score new bars in novelty mode
steps.description: By default the model scores only the bars it was fitted on. To score a fresh bar as it arrives, it is switched to novelty mode, where the fitted bars are the reference crowd and the new bar is compared with them.
steps.inExample: The newest bar is scored against the 50,000 stored bars without being added to them.

useFor.task: Finding odd bars in a market with several moods
useFor.example: Flagging a bar that is strange for a quiet afternoon even though its volume would be normal at the open, because the comparison is made locally.
Dropping the few percent of 5-minute MNQ bars whose features are locally isolated before fitting a model.

useFor.task: Spotting a new kind of bar
useFor.example: Raising a warning when the current bar has no close neighbours among past bars, such as a regime the model has not seen.

useFor.task: A second opinion for another anomaly detector
useFor.example: Running it alongside an isolation forest and reviewing bars that both flag.

avoidWhen: You have millions of bars and need fast scoring; finding neighbours for every bar becomes slow, so an isolation forest is the better choice at that scale.
You have many features that are mostly noise; distances between points become unreliable in many dimensions, so reduce the features first or use a method that does not rely on distances.

example.scenario: A 5-minute MNQ bar closes during a quiet midday stretch. The Local Outlier Factor model, fitted on a year of bars and set to look at 20 neighbours, is asked how out of place the bar is compared with similar bars.

input.summary: Three scaled features describing the bar that just closed, plus the neighbour count.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 5-minute bar closed, shown for reference and not used as a feature.

fields.name: range against average true range
fields.meaning: The bar's high-to-low range compared with the typical recent range; slightly below normal.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: Trading volume was far heavier than the recent norm; more than three times as large.

fields.name: move from open to close
fields.meaning: The bar barely moved, even though volume was heavy.

fields.name: neighbour count
fields.meaning: How many nearest past bars the model compares against.

output.summary: A local outlier factor and a flag for the bar.

fields.name: local outlier factor
fields.meaning: How much more spread out the bar is than its neighbours; 1 means it fits in.

fields.name: typical factor for normal bars
fields.meaning: The level seen for ordinary bars in the fitted data.

fields.name: flag
fields.meaning: The factor is above the cutoff of about 1 and a half set at the top 1 percent of scores.

example.reading: Heavy volume with almost no price movement is a combination that few past bars share, so the bar stands alone and scores about 2. Look at what happened in the market then, such as a large resting order absorbing trades, before deciding whether to exclude it from training or treat it as information.
